lessons.title: Supplier Terms, Early Payment Discounts and the Real Cost of Trade Credit

children.text: Supplier credit is the largest source of working capital funding in most Indian businesses, larger than the bank limit, and the only one with no sanction letter, no margin requirement and no visible interest rate. That last part is why it gets misused.
Trade credit

is not free. It is either priced into the quote you accepted, or it is charged to you every time you decline a cash discount. This lesson puts a number on it, so that stretching a supplier becomes a calculation rather than a reflex.

markDefs.definition: The credit a supplier gives by allowing payment after delivery. It looks free, but it is priced into the invoice.

children.text: What Declining a Discount Actually Costs

A supplier offers 2% off if you pay within 10 days, otherwise the full amount in 45 days. Decline it and you keep your money for an extra 35 days, at a cost of 2% of the invoice. That is not a 2% annual rate. It is 2% for 35 days.

body.caption: d is the discount rate, D is the discount period in days, N is the net credit period
Declining 2% in 10 days, net 45, costs about 21.3% a year

body.title: Annualised cost of declining each discount (%)

children.text: Every one of these is dearer than a cash credit limit at 9.5%, and the 2% in 10 days, net 30 terms cost an extraordinary 37.2% a year. The last row is the interesting one: 1% for paying 38 days early works out to 9.7%, barely above the cost of borrowing, so it is genuinely marginal and other factors decide it.

body.text: The rule is simple. If the annualised cost of declining the discount is higher than your cost of funds, and you have limit headroom, borrow and take the discount. You are arbitraging a very expensive implicit loan with a cheaper explicit one.

children.text: Doing It At Scale
Sunrise Ceramics buys ₹96 crore of raw material a year on 2% in 10 days, net 45 terms, and has never taken the discount. Its cash credit costs 9.5%. Here is the whole decision in four lines.

body.label: Net gain from taking the discount
body.context: The discount of ₹1.92 crore less ₹0.87 crore of extra interest. This is a pure margin improvement with no change to sales, prices or costs.

children.text: Note what the decision needs: ₹9.21 crore of permanent additional limit. If the cash credit account has no headroom, the arithmetic is irrelevant, and the company keeps paying 21.3% a year because it cannot access money at 9.5%. That is the real cost of running a fully drawn limit.

body.caption: The discount rate at which paying n days early exactly matches a borrowing cost of r

children.text: Run it the other way and the break-even discount for paying 35 days early at 9.5% is about 0.9%. Anything above that is worth taking, anything below is not. That single number is a useful thing for a procurement team to carry into negotiations.

body.title: Should you take it?
body.prompt: A supplier offers a 1.5% discount for paying 40 days earlier than the normal due date. Your business funds itself on a cash credit limit at 11% a year. What is the annualised cost of declining this discount, as a percentage?
body.explanation: The calculation is 0.015 divided by 0.985, times 365 divided by 40, which is about 13.9%. That is comfortably above the 11% cost of funds, so take the discount if the limit has headroom.

children.text: Price and Terms Are One Negotiation

Procurement teams often negotiate price and payment terms separately, and treat a win on either as a win. They are the same negotiation, and the only way to compare quotes is to convert both into one number.

Supplier A quotes ₹100 a unit with 30 days credit. Supplier B quotes ₹97.5 a unit against advance payment. At a funding cost of 10%, paying B 30 days earlier costs ₹0.8 a unit in interest, so B's effective cost is ₹98.3 against A's ₹100. B is cheaper by ₹1.7 a unit, despite demanding cash upfront.

body.text: The reverse is equally common. A supplier who agrees to 90-day terms after resisting often quietly adds 2% to 3% to the price, which is far more than the credit is worth. Always ask for both quotes: the price at your standard terms, and the price at the longer terms. If the supplier cannot separate them, you are being charged for credit without being told the rate.

body.title: When stretching payables is cheap, and when it is not

columns.label: Genuinely low cost
points: The supplier has priced its terms into the quote and applies no discount either way
Your business is a large, valued customer with alternatives available
The extended terms are formally agreed rather than taken unilaterally
The supplier is not a registered micro or small enterprise
You are within the agreed terms, just using all of them

columns.label: Expensive, even though no interest is charged
points: A cash discount is on the table and you are declining it
The supplier quietly raises prices at the next revision to recover the cost
You slip down the allocation list when material is scarce, which costs you sales
Quality and service attention drift to customers who pay on time
The supplier is a registered micro or small enterprise, which brings a statutory interest liability covered in the next lesson

body.title: Three practical points for Indian buyers

children.text: Cash discounts and GST. Where a discount is agreed in advance and linked to specific invoices, it can be handled through a credit note so the taxable value reflects the reduced price. Discounts negotiated after the event are treated differently and often cannot reduce the tax already charged. This is a detail worth confirming with your tax advisor before designing a discount programme, because getting the paperwork wrong turns a 2% saving into a tax dispute.

Dynamic discounting and supply chain finance. Larger buyers run programmes where suppliers choose to be paid early at a sliding discount, or where a bank pays the supplier at the buyer's credit rating while the buyer pays on the original date.
Supply chain finance
is a genuine win for both sides when the buyer is more creditworthy than the supplier, and Chapter 6 covers the mechanics.

markDefs.definition: Supply chain finance. A buyer-arranged programme where a bank pays the supplier early at the buyer's credit rating, and the buyer pays the bank on the original due date.

children.text: Watch your own
days payable outstanding

trend. A rising figure is read by lenders and rating agencies as a liquidity signal, not as a negotiating triumph. If your payable days are climbing while your receivable days are flat, the market conclusion is that you are funding your business by stretching suppliers, which is exactly the pattern Chapter 2 taught you to spot in other companies.

markDefs.definition: Days payable outstanding. The average number of days the business takes to pay its suppliers.

body.title: The hidden rate
body.textWithBlank: Declining a 2% discount for paying 35 days early is equivalent to borrowing at about ___ percent a year, which is far more expensive than a typical cash credit limit.
body.explanation: The calculation is 0.02 divided by 0.98, times 365 divided by 35, which is 21.3% a year. Trade credit taken by declining discounts is among the most expensive money a business can use.

body.title: Which supplier relationship should you pay first?
body.question: Cash is tight this month and you cannot pay every supplier on time. Which should be paid first?
options: The largest supplier by value, since the relationship matters most
A registered micro enterprise whose bill crosses 45 days this week, and any supplier offering a discount worth more than your borrowing rate
The most recent invoices, so the ageing looks cleaner
body.explanation: Two payments have a measurable cost of delay: a registered micro or small supplier, where crossing 45 days triggers a statutory interest liability at a punitive rate, and a discount you are about to forfeit. Everything else is a judgement about relationships. Paying whoever shouts loudest is how businesses end up paying the cheapest credit first and the most expensive credit last.

body.title: The discount you cannot afford to take
body.scenario: Your largest supplier offers a 2% discount for payment in 10 days instead of the usual 45, on annual purchases of ₹96 crore. Your finance head calculates the gain at about ₹1 crore a year and wants to take it. Your cash credit limit is ₹35 crore and is currently drawn to ₹33 crore. Taking the discount needs roughly ₹9.2 crore of additional funding, permanently.
body.prompt: How would you approach this, and what would you propose?
body.modelAnswer:
The arithmetic is right and the conclusion does not follow. A ₹1 crore gain that requires ₹9.2 crore of funding you do not have is not available to you today.

The question is therefore not whether to take the discount, but how to fund it. Three routes are worth testing.

First, ask the bank for an enhancement. A ₹9.2 crore increase justified by a documented ₹1.05 crore of annual savings is one of the easier credit cases to argue, because the facility repays its own cost several times over. Expect to bring margin money, and expect the assessment to look at your drawing power, not just the story.

Second, ask the supplier for a middle option. Many will offer a smaller discount for a shorter acceleration, for example 1% for paying in 20 days instead of 45. That needs roughly ₹6.6 crore of funding rather than ₹9.2 crore, and still beats your cost of funds comfortably.

Third, take it selectively rather than fully. Apply the discount to whatever portion of monthly purchases your headroom supports, perhaps 20% to 30% of invoices, and capture a proportionate share of the gain with no new borrowing at all. Most suppliers accept invoice-level discounting.

And note the lesson underneath. A permanently drawn cash credit limit does not just cost interest, it costs you every opportunity that requires cash. That is the hidden price of running at 94% utilisation, and it belongs in the conversation about limit sizing, not in a discount debate.

body.title: Build a payables policy worth having
steps: List every supplier's stated terms, including any cash discount, and confirm them against what you actually pay.
Compute the annualised cost of every discount on offer, and compare it with your current cost of funds.
Identify which suppliers are registered micro or small enterprises, since their payment timing is a legal matter, not a commercial one.
Ask for quotes at two payment terms on significant purchases, so the price of credit is visible.
Set a payment run calendar and stick to it, since predictability is worth more to a supplier than speed.
Never take extended terms unilaterally: negotiate them, document them, and then use them fully without apology.
Track days payable outstanding and on-time payment percentage monthly, and watch both trends together.
Review annually whether a supply chain finance programme would let your suppliers get paid earlier without costing you cash.

body.text: Supplier credit has an interest rate. It is just written on a discount schedule instead of a sanction letter. Compute it before you decide that stretching a supplier is the cheap option.

points: Trade credit is never free: it is either priced into the quote or charged through a forfeited cash discount.
The annualised cost of declining a discount is the discount divided by one minus the discount, times 365 divided by the extra days gained.
Common terms such as 2% in 10 days, net 45 cost over 21% a year to decline, far above any bank limit.
Taking discounts at scale needs permanent additional funding, so a fully drawn cash credit limit blocks the saving entirely.
Compare supplier quotes by converting price and terms into one effective cost per unit at your funding rate.
A supplier who concedes longer terms often recovers the cost in the price, so always ask for both quotes.
Stretching payables has costs that never appear as interest: allocation priority, service attention, price revisions and, for registered small suppliers, statutory interest.
